title: Sets, Groups and Chunks
focus: Linear where you expected n log n, list surgery in fixed-size blocks, and merging identities.

cards.title: Longest Consecutive Sequence
patterns: Start only from a run's beginning
cards.trigger: Consecutive runs in an unsorted array, and sorting is explicitly forbidden.
cards.recall: Write it from memory. Then answer the complexity question that decides whether you actually understand it: there is a while loop inside a for loop. Why is this O(n) and not O(n^2)?
useWhen: Longest consecutive sequence in O(n)
Group numbers into consecutive ranges
Missing ranges, summary ranges
Any run-detection where sorting is banned or too slow
Union find alternative when the relation is 'differ by one'
template: continue                 # not the start of a run, skip
while x + length in s:       # walk the run once
# The guard is everything. Without `if x - 1 in s: continue` this is O(n^2)
# because every element of a long run re-walks the whole run.
keyInsights: Each run is walked exactly once, from its unique starting element. Total inner work is bounded by n, so the whole thing is linear
Iterating the set rather than the list avoids re-processing duplicates
This is the canonical 'inner loop that is still amortised linear' proof. Practise saying it in two sentences
cards.trap: 'Sort it, it is easier.' It is, and it is O(n log n), and the problem explicitly asks for linear. Offering the sort as a fallback is fine; leading with it is not.

cards.title: Reverse Nodes in k-Group
cards.trigger: Linked list surgery on fixed-size blocks, where a partial final block must be left alone.
cards.recall: Write it from memory. Then answer: the hard part is not the reversal, it is the reconnection. Which three pointers do you need to hold on to across each group?
useWhen: Reverse nodes in k-group
Swap nodes in pairs, the k = 2 case
Rotate a list by k, or partition around a value
Reorder a list, odd-even linked list
Any block-wise list transformation
template: # 1. find the kth node from group_prev; stop if the group is short
# 2. reverse the group, seeding prev with what comes AFTER it
# 3. reconnect: old head of the group is now its tail
keyInsights: Seeding `prev` with `group_next` instead of None is what wires the reversed block to the rest of the list automatically
The old first node of the group becomes the new `group_prev`, and you must capture it before you overwrite the link
Counting to k first is what leaves a short final group untouched. Reversing first and undoing is far messier
cards.trap: 'Do it recursively.' It is shorter to write and O(n/k) stack space. Say the space cost rather than presenting recursion as strictly better.

cards.title: BST Lowest Common Ancestor
cards.trigger: LCA where the tree is a BST, so ordering tells you which way to go.
cards.recall: Write the iterative version from memory. Then answer why the split point is necessarily the LCA, in one sentence, using only the BST property.
useWhen: LCA in a BST
Insert into a BST at the correct position
Closest value in a BST, or the k closest
Range sum of a BST, prune whole subtrees
Any BST query where a comparison discards a subtree
template: if p.val < node.val and q.val < node.val:
node = node.left        # both strictly smaller: LCA is left
elif p.val > node.val and q.val > node.val:
node = node.right       # both strictly larger: LCA is right
return node             # they straddle, or one IS this node
# Range sum with pruning, same idea:
if node.val < lo:  return range_sum(node.right, lo, hi)   # skip left entirely
if node.val > hi:  return range_sum(node.left,  lo, hi)   # skip right entirely
return node.val + range_sum(node.left, lo, hi) + range_sum(node.right, lo, hi)

problem.name: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree

keyInsights: The first node where p and q fall on opposite sides is the deepest node containing both. That is the whole proof
It is O(1) space iteratively, which the general binary tree version cannot achieve
If they said BST and you wrote the general recursive LCA, you left the constraint on the table. They notice
cards.trap: 'What if one of the nodes is not in the tree?' The split-point walk happily returns a node anyway. You need a verification descent, and they will ask.

cards.title: Counting Combinations
cards.trigger: Count the ways to reach a total, where two orderings of the same multiset are the same way.
cards.recall: Write coin change II from memory. Then, without looking, write the permutation-counting version too, and say in one sentence what the loop order does.
useWhen: Count ways to make an amount with unlimited coins
Combination sum IV, which is actually the permutation version
Count ways to climb stairs with variable step sizes
Dice roll sums, and any ordered-versus-unordered counting
Any 'how many ways' knapsack
template: # COMBINATIONS: {1,1,2} and {2,1,1} are the SAME. Coin outer.
dp[0] = 1                       # one way to make zero: take nothing
for c in coins:                 # fix an order on the coins
# PERMUTATIONS: {1,1,2} and {2,1,1} are DIFFERENT. Amount outer.
if x <= t: dp[t] += dp[t - x]
keyInsights: Coin outer means each coin type is considered once and forever, which forces a canonical order on the multiset. That is what removes duplicates
Amount outer lets every coin be the last one added at every step, which is exactly counting orderings
LeetCode names Combination Sum IV misleadingly. It counts permutations. Read the examples, not the title
cards.trap: 'Now the coins are limited to one each.' That is 0/1 counting, so it is a backwards capacity loop again. Three loop patterns, all one line apart.

cards.title: Union Find over Identities
patterns: Map arbitrary keys to integer ids
Collect by root at the end
cards.trigger: Merge groups keyed by something that is not an index: emails, names, equations, currencies.
cards.recall: Sketch accounts merge from memory. Then answer the modelling question, which is the actual difficulty: what is a node, what is an edge, and why do you union every email to the first email of its account?
useWhen: Accounts merge, synonymous names, similar sentences
Evaluate division, currency conversion graphs
Number of operations to make a network connected
Redundant connection, detect the edge that creates a cycle
Any grouping over non-integer keys
template: union(email, first)       # every email joins this account's group
return [[owner[root]] + sorted(emails) for root, emails in groups.items()]
keyInsights: Emails are nodes, and each account is a star of edges to its first email. That modelling step is the entire problem
Names cannot be nodes because two people can share a name. Only emails are unique identities
A dictionary-backed DSU with `setdefault` avoids a separate id-assignment pass and reads cleanly
cards.trap: 'Do it with DFS on a graph instead.' You can, and the graph construction is the same insight. If you cannot state the node and edge model, neither approach will work.
